**Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair**
Neruda's most famous collection, published in 1924 when he was 19. It contains twenty numbered love poems followed by a final poem, "The Song of Despair." Almost every question ends by calling Neruda the "Chilean poet" of this book.

**"In you everything sank!"**
The refrain repeated throughout "The Song of Despair," the last poem in *Twenty Love Poems*. The speaker also calls the lost lover a "pit of debris" and a jar that held "infinite tenderness."

**"Tonight I can write the saddest lines"**
The opening line of Poem 20, the second-to-last poem in *Twenty Love Poems*. Examples of the "saddest lines" include "the night wind revolves in the sky and sings" and "She loved me, sometimes I loved her too." The poem also contains the line "Love is so short, forgetting is so long."

**"It is the hour of departure"**
The closing refrain of "The Song of Despair," which opens with "The memory of you emerges from the night around me." In the same poem the speaker calls himself "deserted like the wharves at dawn" and defines the hour of departure as the "hard cold hour which the night fastens to all the timetables."

**Elemental Odes**
Neruda's 1954 collection of short-lined odes to ordinary things. Subjects include the onion, praised as a "heavenly globe, platinum goblet" that can "make us cry without hurting us," as well as tomatoes, which "invade the kitchen," and conger chowder, a dish in which "you may know heaven."

**"Ode to My Socks"**
An ode to a pair of socks knitted for Neruda by Maru Mori. He says they were made from "threads of twilight and goatskin" and compares his feet to "two fish," "two long sharks," "two immense blackbirds," and "two cannons." It ends with the moral that "beauty is twice beauty and what is good is doubly good."

**"Body of a Woman"**
The first poem in *Twenty Love Poems*. It describes the beloved's "white hills, white thighs" and his own "body, savage and peasant, undermining you." The speaker says he was "lonely as a tunnel" and that "to survive I forged you like a weapon."

**Canto General**
Neruda's 1950 epic about the history of the Americas, with sections such as "The Conquistadors" and "The Liberators" and the canto "America, I Do Not Invoke Your Name in Vain." He finished it while hiding from Chile's government, which had outlawed communism. He escaped on horseback across the Andes (described in *The Grapes and the Wind*) and later traveled to Paris on the passport of Guatemalan novelist Miguel Ángel Asturias. He won the 1971 Nobel Prize in Literature.

**"The Heights of Macchu Picchu"**
A twelve-part poem in *Canto General*, inspired by Neruda's 1943 visit to the Inca ruins in Peru. It begins with the speaker moving "from air to air, as through an empty net." The last section opens "Arise to birth with me, my brother" and asks the dead laborers to "speak through my words and my blood."

**"Ode to the Artichoke"**
An ode in *Elemental Odes* about a "tender hearted" vegetable dressed like a "solitary man of war among these frail vegetables." At the end, a woman named María buys it at the market along with "a pair of shoes, a white cabbage and a bottle of vinegar," then cooks and eats it.

**"White Bee"**
A poem from *Twenty Love Poems* in which the speaker tells a "white bee" that "you buzz in my soul, drunk with honey." It repeats the refrain "Ah you who are silent!" and includes the lines "I am the one without hope, the word without echoes" and "In my barren land you are the final rose."

**"Ode to a Large Tuna in the Market"**
An ode describing a big tuna for sale at a market as a "torpedo from the ocean." Neruda praises it as "the only true machine of the sea: unflawed, undefiled," a creature that "lived through the sea's truth."

**"A Dog Has Died"**
A late Neruda poem mourning his dog, whom he buried in the garden "next to a rusted old machine," adding that "some day I'll join him right there." He remembers the dog as "full of the voltage of the sea's movement." Although he "never believed in any promised heaven," the speaker believes "in a heaven I'll never enter."

**"The United Fruit Company"**
A political poem in *Canto General* attacking the American banana corporation's power over Central America. It opens with "Jehovah" dividing the world among companies like "Coca-Cola Inc." The company "abolished free will," and the dictators it supports are called "damp flies of modest blood and marmalade."

**"Every Day You Play"**
Poem 14 of *Twenty Love Poems*. It opens "every day you play with the light of the universe," and the speaker promises to bring "rustic baskets of kisses." In W. S. Merwin's translation it ends "I want to do with you what spring does with the cherry trees."
